new_statements.quote: Acento de intensidad: en la primera sílaba de la última raíz de una palabra; no es predecible en términos fonológicos puesto que una raíz puede tener una o dos sílabas en palabras nativas –más en préstamos– y puede llevar prefijos léxicos que no aceptan el acento (un signo de más, +, aparece antes de la sílaba tónica en los ejemplos cuando el acento no recae en la primera)
new_statements.translation: Intensity (dynamic) stress: on the first syllable of the last root of a word; it is not predictable in phonological terms, since a root may have one or two syllables in native words – more in loanwords – and may carry lexical prefixes that do not accept stress (a plus sign, +, appears before the stressed syllable in the examples when the stress does not fall on the first one).
new_statements.citation: Smith Stark, Thomas C. 2007. Los préstamos entre el español y el zapoteco de San Baltasar Chichicapan. UniverSOS: Revista de Lenguas Indígenas y Universos Culturales 4: 9-39. §2.2 'Los sistemas fonológicos del español y del zapoteco', example (5).
new_statements.locator: p. 18 (PDF page 18 of the whole-issue file; example (5) under §2.2)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (whole-issue UniverSOS 4, 2007; Smith Stark article at printed pp. 9-39) and its extracted text dump. The quoted passage is present verbatim (only line breaks differ): 'Acento de intensidad: en la primera sílaba de la última raíz de una palabra; no es predecible en términos fonológicos puesto que una raíz puede tener una o dos sílabas en palabras nativas –más en préstamos– y puede llevar prefijos léxicos que no aceptan el acento (un signo de más, +, aparece antes de la sílaba tónica en los ejemplos cuando el acento no recae en la primera)'. Locator correction: example (5) 'Fonemas segmentales del zapoteco de San Baltazar Chichicapan' starts on printed p. 17 = PDF page 18 and the Lari…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is morphologically anchored: it falls on the first syllable of the last (rightmost) root of the word; prefixes (including lexical prefixes) and any non-final root in a compound are unstressed. Because roots are 1-2 syllables (longer in Spanish loans) and prefixes vary, the position is not computable from the phonological string alone. Corroborated first-hand by Benton, Black & Glaser 1997 (SIL-Mexico Workpapers 12), p. 25: 'the initial nucleus of a root will reduce (in stress and/or glottalization) if the root is not the final root in the word', and p. 29: 'When it occurs as the first member of a compound, a noun can have an unstressed allomorph'. The language is also tonal (Smith-Stark 2007 p. 18: tones grave, ascendente, descendente; Benton 1987 p. 72 lists six tones), with stress a separate 'acento de intensidad'.
new_statements.exceptions: Smith-Stark 2007: position is 'no predecible en términos fonológicos' because root length varies and lexical prefixes do not take stress; in the loanword examples stress is marked with + before the tonic syllable whenever it is not word-initial (e.g. ga+mízhi 'camisa', pa+râje 'paraje', sacra+shtân 'sacristán'). Glaser/Black/Benton 1997: non-final roots in compounds have reduced, 'unstressed' allomorphs (e.g. tu'h 'rope' > tu'-kusi'w 'lightning'; naan 'lady' > nan-:swehktya 'mother-in-law').
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root + prefixes; compounds); statement made in a phoneme-inventory sketch preceding a loanword study, not an instrumental study. The Glaser/Black/Benton 1997 evidence is from an AMPLE morphological-parser description (tone-and-stress table (2), pp. 11-12; allomorphy pp. 25, 29).
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Zapotec of San Baltazar Chichicapan (official spelling San Baltazar Chichicápam), district of Ocotlán, Oaxaca = chic1274 exactly; Smith-Stark places it among the 'dialectos vallistas del zapoteco central'. No dialect split involved.

new_statements.quote: ChZ has the following phonemic inventory: fortis stops p, pʷ, t, tʸ, k, kʷ; lenis stops b, bʷ, d, dʸ, g, gʷ; [...] semivowels w, y; tones high (V́), mid (V̄), rising (V̌), and low (not written); laryngeal glottalization (VV), checked glottalization (Vˀ), and long checked glottalization (V:ˀ); and stress (') (penultimate unless written). Fortis consonants in ChZ are phonetically characterized by firm articulation and length immediately after stressed vowels and firm articulation elsewhere.

The reader's quotation matches word for word; its '[..]' stands for the affricat…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record has an empty rule; the existing statement (Smith Stark 2007, p. 18) places stress on the first syllable of the last root of the word and calls it not phonologically predictable (morphological). Benton 1981 gives a positional generalization instead: penultimate unless. For the typical Chichicapan word (aspect/causative prefix + disyllabic root, or bare disyllabic root) the two pick the same syllable (root-initial = penult), so the placement is compatible; what differs is the framing (phonological default plus lexical marking vs. morphological root-initial). They could diverge for prefix + monosyllabic root forms (e.g. gu-za 'bathed', gu-yu:ʔ 'entered', p. 12), where Smith…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is penultimate by default; forms with stress elsewhere are marked with (') in the transcription, i.e. penultimate stress with lexically marked exceptions. The paper does not analyse stress further; stress figures only as a conditioning environment in rules (Rounding: b > bʷ before stressed front vowels, p. 19; Vowel Deletion: an unstressed vowel deletes before a vowel or y, p. 22) and as the site of consonant length (fn 1, fn 6).
new_statements.exceptions: 'penultimate unless written' — non-penultimate stress exists and is written with ('), but no examples of it are discussed; the data tables I checked (p. 12) carry only tone diacritics, no stress marks. Fn 7 (p. 29): mid tone 'usually only occurs on the stressed syllable of recent Spanish loanwords'. Fn 6 (p. 28): fortis obstruents are phonetically long after stressed vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Benton 1981 fn 1 (p. 28): 'Chichicapan Zapotec is spoken in the town of San Baltazar Chichicapan in the district of Ocotlan, Oaxaca, Mexico, and there are approximately 3,000 speakers'; data collected in the town March 1978-August 1979 and at the SIL Ixmiquilpan workshop in 1979. Same variety as the catalog item (Glottolog chic1274, ISO zpv).

readall_conflicts: Mild, framing-level: Benton 1981 (fn 1, p. 28) states stress is 'penultimate unless written', a phonological default with lexically marked exceptions, whereas the catalog's existing statement from Smith Stark 2007 (p. 18) puts stress on the first syllable of the last root and says it is not phonologically predictable. For the bulk of the lexicon (final disyllabic roots, with or without prefixes) both rules select the same syllable, so there is no disagreement on placement; the potential divergence is prefix + monosyllabic root words (Smith Stark: stress on the root, i.e. final; Benton's default: penult, i.e. the prefix), which Benton's data do not settle because his examples carry tone marks only and no explicit stress marks. Smith Stark's is the dedicated later phonological sketch by the language's principal describer, Benton's a one-line inventory footnote in a morphology paper, so the morphological reading remains the better-supported one and Benton's penultimate generalization is best read as its surface shorthand.
